subject: Economics
description: GST mechanics, cess, excise, customs, ad-valorem vs specific, distinction from direct taxes

options.option_text: Goods or services — burden can be shifted to the consumer

questions.explanation: Direct vs Indirect — DIRECT tax (income tax, corporate tax, capital gains, wealth tax) is paid directly by the assessee to the government; burden cannot be shifted. INDIRECT tax (GST, customs, excise) is levied on goods/services, collected by an intermediary (seller), but ultimately borne by the final consumer. India's tax mix has shifted — pre-GST, indirect taxes ~65% of total revenue. Post-GST, ratio became more direct-heavy. Capital tax = direct tax. Goods purchase = pays GST (indirect).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: GST in India operates on the principle of:

options.option_text: Value-added taxation with credit for input taxes (no cascading)
Lump-sum fixed tax irrespective of value

questions.explanation: GST = Value-Added Tax. Each link in the supply chain pays tax only on the VALUE ADDED at that stage; gets Input Tax Credit (ITC) for tax paid on its inputs. Eliminates cascading (tax-on-tax), which was a defect of pre-GST excise + state VAT + service tax + entry tax + octroi. India follows DESTINATION-based GST — tax accrues to the state where the good/service is consumed, not produced. Slabs: 0%, 5%, 12%, 18%, 28% (+cess on demerit goods). Petroleum products + alcohol kept outside GST.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: GST has FOUR component sub-types in India. Which combination is correct?
questions.explanation: Four GSTs based on destination + transaction nature: CGST — Central GST, levied on intra-state transactions, accrues to Centre. SGST — State GST, accrues to State on the same intra-state transaction. IGST — Integrated GST on INTER-state transactions; later split between origin and destination via clearing mechanism. UTGST — for transactions in Union Territories without a state legislature. CGST + SGST = total intra-state rate (e.g., 18% = 9% + 9%). IGST = full rate (e.g., 18%) for inter-state.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: GST Council is a constitutional body under:
questions.explanation: Article 279A inserted by 101st Constitution Amendment Act, 2016 (in force 1 July 2017 with GST). GST Council — Union Finance Minister (chair), Union Minister of State for Finance, Finance Minister (or nominated) of every State + UT with legislature. Decisions need 3/4 majority of votes — Centre has 1/3 weightage, States together 2/3. Recommends rates, exemptions, model GST law, threshold, special rates. Following SC ruling in Mohit Minerals (2022), recommendations are NOT binding but persuasive.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Which of these is a CESS (not a regular tax) levied by the Centre?

options.option_text: Health and Education Cess (4% on direct tax) + Swachh Bharat Cess (earlier)

questions.explanation: Cess — earmarked levy for a specific purpose; goes into a designated fund, NOT shared with states (unlike regular taxes which go through Finance Commission devolution). Health and Education Cess (4%) — added on direct tax liability. Swachh Bharat Cess (0.5%, 2015-17) — went into Swachh Bharat fund. Krishi Kalyan Cess — agriculture. GST Compensation Cess on demerit goods (luxury cars, tobacco) — funds the GST compensation grant to states. Surcharge — different from cess; goes to general revenue.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: Customs duty in India is levied on:

options.option_text: Goods crossing the international border (imports + a few exports)

questions.explanation: Customs Duty — under Customs Act, 1962 + Customs Tariff Act, 1975. Levied at ports/airports/land borders by CBIC officers. Two main types: Basic Customs Duty (BCD), Integrated GST (IGST on imports), Compensation Cess, Anti-Dumping Duty (when foreign goods are dumped at low prices), Countervailing Duty (offsets export subsidies abroad), Safeguard Duty. Used for protectionism (raise BCD on certain goods to support domestic industry — e.g., 2024 increase on smartphones), revenue, regulating trade. Export duty is rare — mostly raw materials (e.g., iron ore).
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: An 'ad valorem' tax is one which is calculated as:

options.option_text: A flat amount per unit (specific tax)
A percentage of the value of the goods or transaction

questions.explanation: Ad valorem (Latin 'according to value') — tax = % × value. Examples: GST (5/12/18/28% of price), Customs ad valorem rate, Stamp duty on property, ad valorem excise on luxury goods. Specific tax = fixed amount per unit (tonne, litre, piece) — e.g., excise on tobacco per stick, road tax per vehicle. Most modern indirect taxes are ad valorem (revenue scales automatically with inflation/economy growth) — but 'sin tax' on cigarettes is sometimes specific to discourage consumption regardless of price.
questions.subject: Economics

questions.stem: GST in India subsumed approximately how many indirect taxes that were previously levied by the Central and State governments combined?
questions.explanation: GST subsumed 17 taxes: 8 Central (Central Excise, Service Tax, CVD, SAD, CST, Excise on medicinal preparations, additional excise on textiles and sugar) and 9 State (VAT, entry tax, luxury tax, entertainment tax, advertisement tax, purchase tax, lottery/betting tax, octroi, State cesses). Option B is wrong — 25 overstates the count and misrepresents the Central/State split.

questions.stem: Which constitutional amendment inserted Articles 246A and 279A into the Indian Constitution, formally enabling the GST framework?
questions.explanation: The 101st CAA, 2016 inserted Art 246A (concurrent GST law-making power), Art 269A (IGST levy), and Art 279A (GST Council), and amended Schedule VII. The 100th CAA (land boundary agreement with Bangladesh) is the most common distractor due to adjacency; the 97th CAA dealt with co-operative societies and the 103rd introduced EWS reservation.

questions.stem: Under the GST framework, Integrated GST (IGST) is levied on inter-State supplies of goods and services. Who collects IGST, and how is the revenue ultimately apportioned?

options.option_text: Origin State collects; revenue is split equally between origin and destination States
Centre collects; revenue is apportioned between Centre and the destination State
Centre collects; entire IGST revenue is retained by the Central Government
Both States collect separately; GST Council arbitrates any revenue surplus

questions.explanation: IGST is collected by the Centre under the IGST Act, 2017. It follows the destination principle: the CGST portion is retained by the Centre, while the SGST-equivalent portion is transferred to the destination (consuming) State. Option C is wrong because the destination State always receives its share — IGST is not a revenue-neutral tool for the Centre alone.

questions.stem: The GST Composition Scheme allows small taxpayers to pay tax at a flat rate with minimal compliance. Which of the following businesses is statutorily INELIGIBLE to opt for this scheme?

options.option_text: A manufacturer of goods with annual turnover below ₹1.5 crore
A restaurant owner (not serving alcohol) with turnover below ₹1.5 crore
A trader engaged in inter-State supply of taxable goods
A retailer of readymade garments with turnover below ₹1.5 crore

questions.explanation: Section 10(2)(b) of the CGST Act explicitly bars any supplier making inter-State outward supplies from the Composition Scheme, regardless of turnover. The scheme is restricted to intra-State suppliers only, since IGST collection across States requires the regular return-filing mechanism. Restaurant owners and intra-State traders are eligible if within the turnover threshold.

questions.stem: Alcoholic liquor for human consumption is deliberately kept outside GST. Which other category of goods still attracts Central Excise duty (not GST) on manufacture as of 2024?

options.option_text: Tobacco products including cigarettes and beedis
Petroleum products such as petrol, diesel, and ATF
Precious metals like gold and silver jewellery
Packaged food items including cereals and pulses

questions.explanation: Five petroleum products — crude oil, natural gas, aviation turbine fuel (ATF), petrol (motor spirit), and high-speed diesel — remain outside GST and continue to attract Central Excise (by Centre) and VAT (by States). Tobacco is the most common wrong answer; it IS under GST at 28% plus a compensation cess. Gold attracts 3% GST, and cereals/pulses attract 0–5% GST.

questions.stem: A 'zero-rated supply' under the IGST Act is fundamentally different from a GST-exempt supply. Which statement accurately captures the critical operational distinction between them?

options.option_text: Zero-rated supplies attract 0% GST; exempt supplies attract 5% — the lowest positive slab
On zero-rated supplies, supplier can claim full ITC refund; on exempt, ITC is unavailable
Zero-rated covers only goods exports; exempt supply covers only domestic services
Zero-rated needs GSTR-1 filing; exempt supplies fall outside the GST return framework

questions.explanation: Zero-rated supply (exports and SEZ supplies under Section 16 IGST Act) levies 0% GST but crucially allows the supplier to claim a refund of Input Tax Credit on all inputs used. Exempt supplies also attract no GST but the supplier must reverse any ITC taken on inputs used for exempt supplies — making the tax cost stick in the supply chain. Option A is wrong because exempt does not mean 5%; it literally means 0% with no ITC flow-through.

questions.stem: A company sells a gift hamper containing chocolates (18% GST), dry fruits (5% GST), and a decorative tin box (12% GST), bundled together as a single assorted pack at one price. What is the correct GST treatment of this transaction?

options.option_text: Composite supply taxed at 18%, since chocolates are the principal element by value
Mixed supply taxed at 18%, being the highest GST rate among its constituent items
Mixed supply taxed at the weighted average GST rate of all three components
Composite supply taxed at 5%, treating dry fruits as the principal natural supply

questions.explanation: A 'composite supply' requires items to be naturally bundled and one to be the principal supply (e.g., transport + insurance). A gift hamper is artificially bundled, so it is a 'mixed supply' under Section 2(74) of CGST Act. Mixed supplies are taxed at the highest rate applicable to any component — here 18% on chocolates. Option C (weighted average) is a common misconception; GST law does not provide for apportionment in mixed supply scenarios.
